utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Good morning to all the interpreters, to the court reporters, to Defence and Prosecution counsel. Good morning to the accused. I want to thank on behalf of Judge Shahabuddeen for the information that you gave to us, and the letter will be given to President McDonald. The registrar mentioned there were some problems here. Mr. Hayman or Mr. Nobilo, will you tell me what the problems are. Apparently, our schedule is going to be somewhat perturbed this morning. Is that true, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Your Honours may have noted the fog this morning. It caused some difficulties, among other things, with getting witnesses here last night. In fact, there were witnesses that didn't get here last night that hoped to get here. But this situation developed late in the evening, and so what we would like to do is we do have some other business with respect to the Defence case, documents and tapes. I am not sure that we will use all of the time today, but I think we have a couple hours of material that can productively be presented. If there is material that doesn't need to be viewed, but can simply be tendered, we certainly invite the Court's comments in that regard. Mr. Nobilo will be making this presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman, for those clarifications. Yes, there is a lot of fog. These are things that happen and sometimes it also happened to the Prosecution witnesses. Mr. Prosecutor, I suppose there are no objections on your part. Should the Defence produce its evidence under a different form?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't comment on how the Defence shall use its allotted time. We can proceed in any way that the Court and counsel wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen. Judge Shahabuddeen agrees. I agree with him. We can proceed that way, that is to try to use the time profitably. If we don't use the entire morning, I can assure Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman that we have enough work to do in our own offices, but the idea is to try not to waste too much time. Mr. Nobilo, are you going to produce evidence? Would you like there to be a discussion about this or do you want to present the materials the way Mr. Harmon did? Exhibit 468. That reminds me. What's 467? I believe you had presented it and there was no Defence comment. Is that right? I am trying to set the rules of the game today so that there be no discussions afterwards. Mr. Harmon, you have already done that. You are a specialist in that business, that is producing additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and thank you very much for that recognition, Judge Shahabuddeen. It's 456 and 406 are the two exhibits, and I see that Mr. Nobilo has a large pile of documents that we will proceed any way the Court feels is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you can begin with your pile of documents. All right. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, as you've seen, the Defence is quick to learn from the Prosecution, but it does not have as many documents as before. I would like these documents to be handed up now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first is 528, the one that deals with Travnik. The one that deals with Novi Travnik, the 21st of May, is D529. And the third, 530, for the document dated in Vitez the 20 May, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy, if you could approach the bench, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The first document is D528 and it is the municipality of Travnik, the government of the municipality of Travnik, section for economy and reparations, and they furnish the Defence with data regarding war reparation, damage caused by the army of BiH and the troops of the MOS in the municipality of Travnik. From this document, and I am speaking of page 1, it appears that; in the municipality of Travnik in 1991 there was 70.402 inhabitants. Of that number, 26.118 were Croats by nationality. From the municipality of Travnik, 19.300 inhabitants left, of which in the area of Nova Bila, which is part of the Novi Travnik area under HVO control, 2.300 refugees settled, and the other Croats that left, that is to say 17.000 Croat refugees, were settled in the neighbouring municipalities of Novi Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca, and also in Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, and foreign countries as well. Of the 19.300 Croats, emanates from the Balkans, 2.206 Croats were exiled by the Serbs and 17.094 were exiled from the municipality of Travnik by the army of the BiH and the troops of the MOS. In the text, furthermore, the facilities devastated are enumerated, and I would like to draw attention to a category of devastated objects, that is houses, Croat houses, damaged between 60 and 80 per cent, and burnt houses, and these owned by Croats. There are 1.450 of these burnt down houses that suffered damages, 1.450, whereas the other houses also enumerated, we have the figures between -- for 20 per cent, 20 to 40 per cent, 40 to 60 per cent and 60 to 100 per cent, and can you see this all on page 1 of that document. Along with this document, the municipality of Travnik sent the Defence examples of citizens sending documents to the Travnik municipality, which was the basis, formed the basis and groundwork of the commission to establish the wartime reparations. They are the individual cases of the individual households. And after a series of individual descriptions of this kind supplied by a number of citizens, we have a table, and the table illustrates the fact that the BiH Army -- from the effects of the BiH Army, over 50 villages suffered damages from that. The table shows the number of inhabitants in each of the villages, the total number of inhabitants, that is the first table, the first column. Then we come to the Croats. The first column, which begins with the number 276, is the total number of inhabitants in one given village. The second column is the number of Croats in each particular village. The third column represents the total number of houses damaged in each village. Then we come to four final columns, which show the damage done, up to 20 per cent, from 20 to 40 per cent, between 40 and 60 per cent, and 60 to 100 per cent damage and destruction. So we see that perhaps the most damaged houses were in Dzelilovac, 123 houses were 100 per cent destroyed; followed by Grahovcici, where 140 houses were completely destroyed; Polje S.Gavrancic with 78 houses, 62 houses and so on. You can read down the table. The next table represents the nationality composition or ethnic composition of the Travnik municipality taken from the population census in 1991. I am not going to comment on that because it is self-explanatory. You can see the population structure there. So that is document D528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards the second chart, is that the one that begins with the Bandol --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Both tables begin with the place called Bandol, but in the second table, the first figure is 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Whereas in Bandol, 276 and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This is a chart, then, showing the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The structure of the population according to the ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. There is a problem with the French transcript. Perhaps we should take a break so we can fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A French transcript problem?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And you want to take a 5-minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The Judges will withdraw. We'll suspend the hearing for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can resume now. Please be seated. Mr. Dubuisson, is the French transcript fixed?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. The problem has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know, French is a fragile language in this Tribunal. It can even be affected by the fog. All right. We can continue now. Mr. Nobilo, have you finished with 528 or do you want to go back to it? Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, I would like to ask my colleague to clarify something on this particular document, and it is in respect of the source of this document because I see on the original a stamp that says "The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna," and I see the on letterhead of the letter to Mr. Nobilo, the Federation of BH, the government of the municipality of Travnik, and just to clarify the issue in the document, if Mr. Nobilo is able to give us that, whether this is the Croatian portion of the federation and whether this is from the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I received this from the department, section for economy of the municipality of Travnik some time in May 1997. Why they don't use the old stamp, I don't know, but the representative of the government, Vlado Lovrinovic, sent this to me, and that's all I know about it. In 1997, he was the representative of the section for economy of the municipality of Travnik. Whether he is that today, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a document from an authority that came out of the Dayton Agreements; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the course of 1997 when the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, but changes go a little more slowly there. Some of them have old stamps, other institutions have the new stamp, but I do know where I got if from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not exist after the Dayton Agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. No, I understand that. See, my document D528, in the English version, says "Bosnia-Herzegovina," the federation of -- so it says "la Federation," the federation, so it is the Croat Muslim federation. I suppose that's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that's exact, and the municipality of Travnik from the Croatian and Muslim federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is the section for economy and reparations for wartime reparation and recording them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My last point of clarification for my colleague, is this the Croat side of the federation that is the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what's important. I suppose that in the municipality of Travnik government, what was its ethnic composition in the government, and this government or municipality of Travnik is the one that set this up because it's got a reparations section, I suppose, in order to make good on damages that were caused during the war; is that right, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour. It is a joint municipality, Croatian and Muslim, but Vlado Lovrinovic, the individual himself, according to his mandate between Muslims and Croats, was appointed a Croat and head of the section for economy and reparations, so the municipality has both Croats and Muslims, but this individual of Croatian nationality, ethnicity, supplied me with those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that at that proper time, that is, in your closing arguments, you can contest the document if you consider it appropriate. For the time being, do you have any other questions, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, did you want to move to the next document now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, it is document D529, and it is, once again, from the section for restoration, building, and urban planning of the municipal council of Novi Travnik, also from the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the district of Central Bosnia. So I received that document at the same time on the 21st of May, 1997, and the subject is information about the devastated buildings in the municipality of Novi Travnik, and the document states that following Article 172 of the Law on General Authority Procedure, this body keeps an official record about the Croats that were expelled from this area by the MOS during the combats between the Croats and the Muslims, and it states furthermore that the Croats were exiled from 26 inhabited villages of the municipality of Novi Travnik, and then it goes on to list the 26 villages of the municipality of Novi Travnik. The first column gives the number of houses and in the second column, the number of inhabitants expelled from each of the villages. You can see that the total from the municipality of Novi Travnik, the number of people expelled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was 4.436 (sic) Croats, and of the 958 houses, 85 per cent were completely destroyed and devastated and have not been capacitated for living. There seems to be an error in the transcript. The figure for the expelled individuals was 4.360 Croats, and of the 958 Croat houses in those villages, 85 per cent were completely destroyed, and it is impossible to live in them. The representative of the section for restoration, building, and urban planning, Josip Udovicic sent the document, and it seems that he used the new stamp of the federation and the district of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If there are no other comments, it's the same author, same source, as the previous one. I suppose you have no comments. Mr. Nobilo, you can then move on to the next document. The one in Serbo-Croat, is that the one you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. We do have a translation, that is to say, the headings of the columns have been translated. Mr. President, the first document has a letter attached to it from the Central Bosnia region, and it is from the same section for renovation and development dated the 20th of May, 1997. The head of the department for renovation and development says that he is sending a list of all the destroyed and damaged houses owned by Croat families, and these were destroyed during the Muslim aggression on Vitez. In that list, the list does not include the houses that are owned by Croat families under the control of Muslims, and there are 10 to 15 per cent of this type of house of the number written down. Then we come to the table itself and the individual columns, and their headings have been translated. The document is entitled "Damage on Building Objects." The first column is the ordinal number and the form number. Then we have the owner of the facility, whether it was a firm or an individual owner. Then we have the local community. It is the municipality of Vitez, in fact. Then we have the local communities of one or more villages. Then we have the degree of destruction, and these ranged from 1 to 6, and the damage expressed in thousands of Deutschmarks. In the final column, we must add in the amount in Deutschemarks and the damage done for the properties of each individual family, and this has been furnished for us by computer by the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen, I don't intend to interrupt, but for purposes of this particular exhibit and to give us a little more insight, I would make an inquiry of counsel in respect of the second to last column which says "Degree of Destruction." They are assigned numbers 1 through 6, and I don't know what the values or percentage of destruction means in respect of 1 through 6, whether the 1 represents the maximum amount or minimum amount of damage, and perhaps Mr. Nobilo could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm not really an expert in this matter, but I seem to feel that the first category is the maximum destruction, although I'm not absolutely sure. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but it seems that in front of 6, it seems that you have higher numbers after columns 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be vice versa. I would suggest that we look at the damages done according to the Deutschemark column which will tell us the order of magnitude of the destruction done, because whether it is 1 or 6, I don't know exactly, but we do have the exact figure in German marks which will illustrate the degree of damage done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I had another question. Perhaps you can answer it, even if not today. Sometimes it's the same name. For example, around the beginning of the last third, I see there's a Kovac Stipo Niko, it's 259 and 263, Kovac Stipo Niko. Category 3, there was, let's say, average damage on the scale, 4.600 -- and he has 4.300. Above it, it says that 248 is Knezevic Anto Jozo of Bukovica, he's got enormous damage because he's in category 6, and then you see under that the same name. Were these property owners with several houses or with farms or something like that? Only you can tell us that. But I think that the Defence has to bring in this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can only assume that this person has several houses. Perhaps he has his main house, and then he has his sheds and barns, and then he has a smaller house, but I can find out and I can give you the exact information, because this was done according to houses, buildings. So if somebody has three houses, then he is mentioned three times, but I better check this out, and then I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know, you have to be very careful, Mr. Nobilo, because when you're talking about reparations, I can tell you this, because I know about this from France, after catastrophes, whether they are earthquakes or wars or hurricanes, this manner for the administration to count the damage, there are people who try to add numbers in. So there are a lot of names, a lot of numbers here. So I'm just pointing this out and asking that you give us some clarification. I suppose it's because they have several houses. Have you finished with this document? Are there any other comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The only other comment I have, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, is the notation in the upper right-hand corner of the computer printout which first indicates the damages in Kuna which is the Croatian currency, and then struck through it is a line that says "DM." My question is, is this the work of the author of this document whose name is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where are you seeing that? What are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Kuna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I can explain. That's the document I received, that is to say, that it was originally expressed in Deutschmarks, and the Kunas were crossed out. I simply imagine that there was a mistake in the computer, and when they saw it printed out, then the author, who sent me the letter and the document, crossed out "Kunas" and put in "DM" because that is the way I received the document because I think that "Kuna" is crossed out, and this is hand-written, "DM," which is German marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Nobilo, you could give more specific indications about that point because, if you don't mind my saying so, this is a very, very rigorous table with very, very specific figures, and suddenly you've got an official who crosses something out and says, "Oh, no, it's in Deutschemarks." It's not being clarified today, not today. But I want to repeat what has already been said, that is, speaking for myself and for Judge Shahabuddeen, I think this has to be clarified. We don't have any powers to give out reparations, not any direct powers, and, therefore, this is an important thing to point out. Do you have any other comments, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Only one last comment and that is, does this document purport to represent exclusively damage to Croat houses because in going through this, very briefly, I see a number of Muslim names. I point out, for example, number 200 and 201. I haven't had time to go through this document in toto. So my question is, are these exclusively Croat houses or is this supposed to represent and does this include, in fact, some Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to the letter that is attached to this computer list, it would appear that these were houses owned by Croat families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For my colleague's assistance, Mr. President, I point out the name "Hrustic." I can point out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it's not the last name that is important. People used to have the same last names earlier on. The first names are the ones that really distinguish between the Croats and the Muslims. So it is the first name that is either Catholic or Muslim, not the last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me just point out, and the names that I pointed out to my colleague include the first name of "Mensud" which, in my impression, is a Muslim name and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What number is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's 201, and the category of damage being 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't see that page. Page 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me try to orient Your Honour with the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a page that begins with "221, Petar Ivisic." That's where my document begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find a way to identify this page. Let me just count the pages, Mr. President, for the moment, and assuming we're in the same order ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The pages are marked in the right-hand corner above.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case, it is -- well, let me see. It's not so clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's page 5. It says "Strana: 4/20/1997."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. That is page 4, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's 201 and 294; is that right? "Hrustic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the numbers I draw the Court's attention and counsel's attention to are numbers 201, 202, and 203, "Naser Hrustic, Muharem Hrustic, Mensud Hrustic." Those appear, to me, to be Muslim names and not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Right. These are Muslim names, but it is also true that in brackets you have Croatian names too, "Veljko Pavlovic, Anto Miskovic," and by "Nasir Hrustic," there is "Ana Totic." In brackets, you have Croatian names only. What does that mean? Whether the house was bought, ownership transferred in one way or the other, that, I do not know, but next to every one of the Muslim names is a Croat name too. But I can address this question to the municipality of Vitez, as all other questions, so we better get their answer, rather than engage in guesswork. So we'll proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that would be very helpful for the clarity of our discussions. Are there any other comments? Do you want to move to 531 now, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There is no 531. These are the only three documents that we introduced today. But we do have some videotapes. Mr. President, our next exhibit would be a videotape. As regards this videotape, you will see that it consists of several parts. I got the first part from the representatives of the Catholic church from Kakanj, and you will be able to see which clergymen filmed this. And then comes video footage from TV Kiseljak speaking of burnt and devastated buildings in Kakanj, Vares and Fojnica, and they also show looting both by Muslim civilians of a Croat village, as well of the military. The video is self-explanatory. There is a title and a date. Here there, there is a sentence or two. The Defence insists on these, and we would truly be pleased if the interpreters could have this interpreted for us, because that would clarify the picture. It is the municipalities of Kakanj, Vares and Fojnica, together with Kiseljak they made up operative group 2 that was commanded by Ivica Rajic, but formally it was under the command of Tihomir Blaskic, that is to say Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, but during one period of time they were certainly under the command of Tihomir Blaskic. So if you agree, could we have the lights dimmed and could we see the videotape, please. You will see the title. First it is the municipality of Kakanj. This is Kakanj. Could we please rewind the tape so we can see the text again, please. I'll read it out. It says: "Kakanj. This video cassette was recorded by Fra Pejo Orsolic, priest in the parish of Kraljeva Sutjeska after the ethnic expulsion of Croats from the area of the municipality of Kakanj." Please proceed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can the interpreters interpret that? I know it's difficult. Would they be able to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner you can see the date, the 5th of July, 1993. The person who made this recording, and he is not a professional, he is just saying who the owners of these houses are. That's all. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the consequences of Muslim vandalism. The Muslim women who did this managed to escape before I managed to film her on camera. This is an approximate interpretation, says the interpreter. These are the few things that remained after the looting. This is the village of Rutici out there. You can see the burnt houses without any roofs. Another house burnt down. This is another part of the village of Okcici, similar pictures. We didn't find any Croat inhabitants of the village of Bakici. This is a burnt house of Fran Stjepan's sister. We are passing through. This old blind woman is one of the few inhabitants left. "What's wrong? Don't cry." This is what is left after those who say that they are humane left. Look at this. This is in a church in -- this is what the MOS threw out when they were here. The famous BiH television is not going to say a word about any of this. This is the level of culture of this humane army. This is excrement in a Catholic church. This is a humane army? This is the upper part of the village of Delevici. None of the inhabitants are left here either. "You've seen a lot, haven't you?" "Yes." Twenty days after the fighting subsided, Croat houses are still burning. Where should people come back? Where to? Our humane Muslim brothers, civilians, are looting the remains of the remains, and the UNPROFOR people are standing there in amazement, together with us, and looking at all of this. However, the Muslim who is doing the looting could not be perturbed. Now a few clips from Alanici. This is the house of Andrija Tunic. Animals were brought upstairs to these rooms and they were even slaughtered up here because there are traces of blood. Look at this. These are bloody pillows. They didn't even take that out. The room is full of excrement too. Dung, traces of blood on the wall. The lighting isn't very good, so you can't see it very well. You can see traces of blood quite well here, though. "Whose house is this?" "Marko, Ilija and Marijan. This is the house of Marko Milos." This is Sime Dujmovic's house. This is a village burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I am not sure whether we -- we plan to take a break. Would it disturb you if we were to interrupt things now and then we could resume after the pause? Because we have a programme for another meeting that we are going to have for about 20 minutes. And we could then resume. I thought perhaps we could wait until the end of the video, but it wouldn't be proper for us not to watch it with the full attention that it should be given. Therefore, if you agree, we are going to break for about 20 minutes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, we can continue viewing the video for the 15th of July, 1993. I think that's right, isn't it? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is a church. Everything has been damaged. This was brought today. This is St. Mark. "Pray for us," it says on the painting. This is a book from the chapel in Paulovici. This was filmed in the village of Tesevo, and this is what remains of the village. It was a very beautiful village once. This was filmed in 1994, in March. This is one of the newer houses, and this is what's left of it. This is a very unusual thing. This village is deserted. This is the farm in Vlahovici. The village of Govedovici, it is now called Hanovici. The houses in the background are the village of Kovaci. They have also been seriously damaged. Who's village is that? That's a Muslim village. It looks as if someone set fire to that house down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if both sides agree, we could speed up the tape because we're looking at houses, and so we'll finish quicker if we speed up the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We agree with the suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We didn't have editorial control over the filmmaker, Mr. President, and we would not have filmed such lengthy clips if we had had control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges have not asked for anything special, and we can watch any evidence presented by either of the parties, but since there is an agreement between the parties, you're the one, Mr. Nobilo, to decide whether or not you want to interrupt the film. I was only permitting myself, so that there be no ambiguity, to ask Mr. Dubuisson to tell us about how many more days of work you have so that we can organise our work properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We could speed up the tape, and when we come to a particular section where you can see that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is looting a Croatian village, we could stop there for awhile and have the normal speed, whereas, we could go through the rest of the tape at a higher speed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "The expelled Croats from the municipality of Vares in Kakanj." That is the text you have on the screen. It says, "The village of Bistrik and Crkvenjak." That's the text on your screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Who took these pictures, Mr. Nobilo? Could you tell us? Is it from a state television programme? Is it a private television station? Can we know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The film was taken by the priest that we saw at the beginning, and his name was written up at the beginning of the tape. Later on, it was mounted by the local television station at Kiseljak, but originally, it was the tape taken by the priest. Here it states precisely that "This is a new film from Vares. This is Kiseljak Television." May we slow down the tape now? This is the village of Pogar. Shall we stop the tape here? We can carry on at normal speed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This portion was now filmed by the local television station of Kiseljak. You have the date, the 4th of November, 1993, and the village of Pogar. The village of Pogar is in the municipality of Vares. These are the units of the BH army. You'll be able to clearly see the insignia at some point, and this is the point at which they are taking away things from the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we do not have to have the second break but just work until 1.30 without a break, unless there's an objection on the part of the interpreters. No objection? All right. Thank you very much. I'm not saying that their work is easier, but perhaps we could gain some time. Okay. We can continue then without a break until 1.30. Is there no sound for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Probably because we decided to speed it up, but more or less, there's nothing to hear. The video is self-explanatory, so there really isn't a soundtrack, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If the interpreters can hear something, I don't quite agree with Mr. Nobilo, the soundtrack is important. Thank you. I thank the interpreters for their explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is very hard to discern the sound because you can only hear background noise rather than words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The units should be lined up. They should take off their arm bands and hand them over to the commander. Who sent this? I'd kill someone for this. I found it under the bed. Edited by Television Kiseljak. Fojnica, village of Bakovici, village of burned down houses by the BH army, the 7th Muslim Brigade, the 110th Mountain Brigade, the Special Unit Dzo, the municipality burned down of Fojnica, devastated and burnt down houses. Our colleague, Marinko, was one of the first to get into the burned out village. The Muslims left the whole place mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Selo Bakovici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is the village of Bakovici, the house of Nikola Bosnjak. Burned down and devastated Croatian houses. They were looted too. Tiles were broken down. Everything was stolen, electricity equipment, everything. We never found anything in these houses, not even clothes or footwear, nothing. The Catholic cemetery above the village, while the fighting was going on in the town of Fojnica, our soldiers were buried there. This is yet another reason for us to have Bakovici remain Croatian once and for all. Our team, nevertheless, managed to film as much as possible. These are war crimes. This was guided by feelings of hatred for everything Croatian. They forget that our wish to return home is much stronger than anything they can feel. We want to build an even better Bakovici. You can also see graffiti by the semi-literate members of the Dzamahirija. They tried to turn Bakovici into a Dzamahirija. Units from Foca and Visegrad were there too. Dzo is probably the most popular amongst all of them belonging to the special units. We are going back towards Luzina from the village of Bakovici. The wild MOS units did terrible things here too. They burned down. They looted. This makes us very sad, but we have to show that we are not a genocidal people, as they want to depict us. Although they destroyed our homes, the mosque in Luzina still remains intact. There is only one single house that remained intact, the one that belongs to the mentally retarded Ivica Gatic, and let it be, because this is part of our cultural, architectural heritage, and any state would protect it. This used to be the house of the late Pero Glavocevic. Thirty years ago, a girl lived there happily as her father and mother were building a house in Sarajevsko Polje. Her grandmother told her nothing remained, and there are only two little teapots there, nothing else, but they still go by the Catholic principle of forgiveness, and the only thing that we can do is ask why. No waterworks, no nothing, but the story about the cross is a bit different. There was a wooden cross in the middle of Tjesilo, a memorial, and it was a memento of times past. The wooden cross, they tried to burn it down, but they didn't manage to. Marijan found it. And whenever they come and whenever they come and do something, they do not respect anything that belongs to other people, notably Croatian things, and then Marijan finds the cross. And God gave this beautiful village, and that beauty is still there, in spite of all the devastation. As we sit in front of Marijan's house, and he is filling it with heavenly water, and the snowy mountain tops are there, and it is quite clear that life will prevail here, in spite of everything. I always wanted to come back to my own home, and I would bring water from Bakovici. What can I do? Other people like being in other people's houses and perhaps they have reasons for doing so or they can't afford it or whatever, but people cannot live off their pensions or whatever. So these are problems. But even if you invest a little, people can come back. And if they don't want to come back, let it be. Before Marijan, Ilija and Mato Mijatovic, brothers, were the first to return. They were persistent, even obstinate, and they managed to rebuild their houses, to bring the livestock back, and here they are living on their own land. Someone is going to say it was easy for them. They were better off when they were refugees than we were. Then there is the story of other people who were in Kiseljak and who tried to do their best in order to keep the land and the orchards going. Things will be better, and his son works in Austria and they are going to do whatever they can. Well, we are going to do whatever is possible. Fifteen days ago I decided what to do and then see what this looks like now. Can you see my garden? And me and this little girl of mine, see what we've done. That's the only thing I can tell you. That's it. I haven't got much time to talk. Marijan is impatient by nature, and it's not easy for him to take things that are illogical. He wonders why SFOR or somebody else does not have the same yardsticks for reconstructing Croatian villages, as well as those of others. However, life will go on at Piescevo either with the help of the International Community or not. You should go there and you should see the scenic beauty there that is God given. Production television Kiseljak, 13th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think that that would be all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that the end of a part of your documentary evidence for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we shall be presenting some other documents, but we have finished for today. However, we would like to hear the position of the Court on a certain problem. We showed videotapes today as we received them on the ground in Bosnia, and the Defence did not edit them in any way. We learned from the comments and objections made by the Prosecution when we give only partial evidence, therefore, we felt it was incumbent upon us to show the tapes in their entirety. However, we are going to waste too much time if we do so. We think that in the future we show only relevant parts of these videotapes, a minute or two or three. Can we have that kind of a ruling by the Trial Chamber so that we don't have to show the video footage in its entirety, because this was not really recorded by professionals. It was done by people who are not very knowledgeable about editing or anything, and their films are not exactly dynamic. Because the Defence has a very large number of videotapes and we would be glad to make the Court aware of all the relevant parts, but if we were to show everything, we would require several months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Several months. That would be not a very good thing for your cause. I know that Mr. Dubuisson is keeping track of the time. How much time is left?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are about 22 days left for the Defence to complete its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It shall include the testimony of the accused. Of course that issue was always problematic, that is, what's considered to be relevant, what isn't. In my country things are done a little differently in courts, but we have to adopt ourselves to the procedural Rules that are in effect here. Let me turn to the Prosecution and ask what they think. Mr. Harmon, you see what the problem is. There is a video cassette, you take out a part, they say it is relevant. Perhaps if you were to know the source and had the cassette, perhaps you might in your final argument show, for instance, that, yes, this part was relevant for the Defence but we have objections. But I don't know. Perhaps we can find a solution together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman run their case is their business, Mr. President. We are certainly not interested in watching hours and hours of tapes with various scenes that are in 1998, 1997, in 1996. We would certainly, in co-operation with the Defence, if they have relevant portions of tapes they want to show, they can show those tapes, and if they would make the rest of the tapes available to us, we could see if there are other portions of those particular tapes that are of interest to us and possibly to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wonder whether the solution wouldn't be to have the Defence present the relevant parts, but to identify the cassette, to state what its source is, and perhaps make -- actually, to make it available to the Prosecutor who can look at it if he wants to. This is a problem that we have with written documents. You saw that the other day. You showed some of the parts of a decree which you considered to be relevant, and the Prosecution asked that the entire decree be provided. I will turn to my colleague and friend Judge Shahabuddeen to have his opinion on the question. Just a moment, please. Judge Shahabuddeen. Judge Shahabuddeen would agree with what I suggest. That is, the Defence would organise its case as it likes, show the first images of the cassette to show who filmed it, how it was filmed, when it was filmed, and, possibly, Mr. Nobilo, make some comments. Then we could show the relevant parts, but the entire cassette would be made available to the Prosecution. And by the final arguments the Prosecution might be able to say, during those arguments, "I would like to point out that Mr. Nobilo showed this or that picture of a destroyed monastery but did not say that in this cassette," et cetera. Is that a solution that would be satisfactory to everybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that would be a satisfactory solution, if we get the complete cassette, if we so desire. We have done that in the past with the Defence, and we will certainly request that the same procedure be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would first like to thank Judge Shahabuddeen and then thank both of the parties for co-operation. Perhaps we should move into private session just so that we can deal with the organisation of our work before we leave perhaps a few minutes earlier today. Are we in private session? Yes, we are. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 2 1:15 p.m. sine die. 25
